title: Exploring Our Unexplored Weaknesses
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Taking Bruna Martinuzzi's figure of the Mensch as his starting point, Stuart argues that the teacher who wants great teaching to flow from them has to do interior work first, and that the most useful interior work is the deliberate examination of one's own weaknesses. He proposes three questions - where am I weak, what's beneath that weakness, how can I improve - and then models them on himself in public. The weakness he names is Survival Mode: last-minute lessons, morning-of copier runs, the permanent sense of catching up. Procrastination is one strand, and he is candid that email is the hardest case because it is both real work owed to real people and a convenient escape from writing or planning. But the larger root he identifies is yes-itis, which he traces to three underdeveloped capacities: estimating the true emotional, cognitive, and temporal cost of a commitment; clarity about what he is there to do in each of his roles; and knowledge of which work matters most outside the classroom, where he admits things remain foggy. The piece ends without a fix, treating the diagnosis itself as the gain.
points: Stuart's diagnostic frame is a three-question sequence - where am I weak, what's beneath that weakness, how can I improve - which pushes past symptom-naming to cause.
His account of email is the sharpest observation here: a task can be simultaneously a genuine obligation to dignified people and a socially acceptable form of procrastination.
He locates chronic overcommitment not in weak willpower but in three underdeveloped capacities - cost estimation, role clarity, and knowing which work matters most.
He notes that he has sorted out what matters most on the teaching side but not outside the classroom, and reads his own Survival Mode as the evidence of that gap.
The closing reframe is worth keeping: finding the areas where one must improve is treated as a delight rather than an indictment, which is what makes the examination repeatable.
quotes: The Mensch [teacher] has a tremendous willingness to learn from everything and everyone. He or she seeks feedback and is not blindsided by unexplored weaknesses.

To be the kind of teacher from whom great teaching tends to flow, the internal work is where it's at. A piece of this work is, I think, the exploration of one's weaknesses, as Martinuzzi suggests above.

One of the weaknesses I want to explore in myself this school year is my tendency to live in a state we all know: Survival Mode. Last minute lessons, morning-of trips to the copier, constantly feeling as if we're just catching up.

A sliver of my weakness is procrastination — letting my work time slip into time-wasting pursuits like unconstrained news reading, or “real quick” Twitter checks, or undisciplined email management. That last one is tricky because email is something I need to do thoughtfully — after all, there are dignified human beings on the other ends of many of those messages — but it's also something that I can use as a means for procrastinating.

But it's far from the whole. I suspect a huge additional part is that I still say yes to too many things: too many meetings, too many efforts that I support, too many extended conversations with colleagues I admire.
The work continues then — joyfully so. It is a great delight to find the areas in which one must improve. How terribly boring all of this would otherwise be.
